scenes.heading: Garbage Collection & GC Tuning
scenes.narration: Let's take a deep look at Go's garbage collector and the two knobs you actually reach for when tuning it.

scenes.heading: One concurrent tricolor cycle
steps: Pacer triggers at the heap goal
Brief STW: enable the write barrier
scenes.narration: Go's collector is concurrent, non-moving, and non-generational tricolor mark-and-sweep. The pacer starts a cycle when the heap reaches its goal, then a brief stop-the-world enables the write barrier. Marking runs concurrently with your program, coloring reachable objects, and a second brief pause finishes marking. Finally sweep reclaims the unreachable white objects. The two stop-the-world pauses are typically sub-millisecond.

scenes.heading: The two tuning knobs
items: GOGC: heap-growth ratio, default 100 means collect when the heap doubles
GOMEMLIMIT: a soft total-memory cap, ideal for containers
Best of all: allocate less so the GC has less to do
scenes.narration: You rarely call the collector directly — you pace it. GOGC is the heap-growth ratio: the default of one hundred triggers the next cycle when the live heap has doubled. GOMEMLIMIT, added in Go 1.19, sets a soft memory cap and makes the runtime collect harder to stay under it, which is perfect for containers. But the cheapest collection is one that never has to scan an object you didn't allocate.

scenes.heading: Bounding memory in a container
scenes.narration: In a container with a one-gibibyte hard limit, you leave headroom so the collector reacts before the OOM killer does. Here we disable the GOGC ratio trigger with set-GC-percent minus one, then set a soft cap around nine hundred mebibytes. Now the runtime collects aggressively as the heap approaches that cap, instead of ballooning until the pod is killed.

scenes.text: The GC only reclaims unreachable objects — a growing cache you still reference is a logical leak it can't fix.
scenes.narration: Remember that the collector reclaims only unreachable objects. A map cache that grows forever, or a slice of pointers you never nil out, stays live to the GC — that's a logical leak no tuning can fix. Reduce allocations first, use gctrace and pprof to diagnose, and bound your caches.
